chapters.title: Chapter 1: Thinking Like a Hedger, Not a Trader

lessons.title: A Quick Options Refresher for Investors: Calls, Puts, Premium, and Expiry

children.text: Every year, some investor opens the Nifty option chain on Kite intending to buy a put for protection and taps S instead of B. They have just sold a put. Instead of insurance, they have written an insurance policy for someone else, and taken on the exact crash risk they were trying to get rid of. This lesson is a fast, investor-focused refresher on the four building blocks: calls, puts, premium and expiry. If you took Options Trading from Zero, treat it as a quick recap through a hedger's eyes. Nothing in the rest of this course works unless these basics are automatic.

body.text: An option buyer pays a premium for a right. An option seller collects that premium and takes on an obligation. Hedgers mostly buy rights. The only obligation a hedger should take on is one already covered by something they own.

children.text: Calls and Puts: Rights, Not Obligations

markDefs.definition: The asset an option is based on, such as the Nifty 50 index or shares of a company like Infosys.
The fixed price at which the option buyer can buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying.
The person who sells an option. They receive the premium and must honour the contract if the buyer's option ends in the money at expiry.

children.text: An option is a contract on an
underlying
at a fixed
strike price
until a fixed expiry date. There are only two kinds, and each has a buyer and a
writer
Call option:
the right to buy the underlying at the strike. It gains value as the price rises above the strike.
Put option:
the right to sell the underlying at the strike. It gains value as the price falls below the strike.
Two types, two sides. That gives exactly four positions. Each one has a clear use, or a clear danger, for someone who already owns stocks or mutual funds.

body.caption: The four basic option positions, seen from an investor's side of the table

cells: Right to sell at the strike
The core hedge: insurance on shares or a portfolio you own
Obligation to sell at the strike
Very large if you do not own the underlying
Covered call: earn premium on shares you hold, giving up upside above the strike
Right to buy at the strike
Lock in an entry level when you are sitting in cash and fear missing a rally
Obligation to buy at the strike
Adds downside risk. The opposite of insurance, so rarely a hedging tool

body.text: A short put and a long put both have the word "put" in them, and they are opposites. A long put pays you when the market falls. A short put costs you when the market falls, on top of whatever your portfolio already lost. Before placing any order, read the confirmation screen and check that it says BUY.

body.title: Pick the insurance
body.question: You own ₹6 lakh of Infosys shares and want to limit your loss if the stock falls sharply over the next month. Which position does that?
body.explanation: Buying a put gives you the right to sell at the strike, so it gains value as the stock falls and offsets your loss. Selling a put adds more downside. Buying a call does nothing for a fall. Selling a call brings in a little premium but gives almost no protection in a sharp fall.

children.text: A Protective Put on a Stock, Worked Through

Suresh, a chartered accountant in Mysuru, holds 400 Infosys shares at ₹1,500, worth ₹6,00,000. Results are due in three weeks and he is worried. One Infosys option lot is 400 shares in this example, so one put covers his whole holding. He buys one lot of the 1,450 put expiring after results at ₹17. His cost is 17 × 400 = ₹6,800.

body.caption: Suresh's 1,450 put on its own, per share. It loses at most ₹17 and gains ₹1 for every rupee Infosys falls below 1,433 (the breakeven).
Suresh's 400 Infosys shares at expiry, with the 1,450 put bought at ₹17 (illustrative)

children.text: However far Infosys falls, Suresh's loss stops at ₹26,800: the ₹50 gap from ₹1,500 to the strike on 400 shares (₹20,000) plus the ₹6,800 premium. If results are good, he keeps all the upside minus ₹6,800. It is the same shape as Ananya's Nifty hedge in Lesson 1, just on a single stock.
Premium: Intrinsic Value Plus Time Value

markDefs.definition: The amount an option would be worth if it expired right now. It can never be negative.
The part of the premium above intrinsic value. It reflects the chance of a favourable move before expiry and shrinks to zero by expiry day.

children.text: Every option premium splits into two parts.
Intrinsic value
is what the option is worth if exercised this second.
Time value
is everything else: the price of possibility. For a hedger, time value is the real cost of insurance, because it melts away whether or not anything bad happens.

body.latex: \begin{aligned} \text{Call intrinsic} &= \max(S - K,\ 0) \\ \text{Put intrinsic} &= \max(K - S,\ 0) \\ \text{Time value} &= \text{Premium} - \text{Intrinsic value} \end{aligned}
body.caption: S = current price of the underlying, K = strike price
A simplified Nifty option chain: Nifty at 25,000, about four weeks to expiry (illustrative premiums)

body.text: Two patterns to notice. First, time value is largest at the strike closest to the current price (25,000) and shrinks as you move away in either direction. Second, the 26,000 put shows a small negative time value (*). That happens with deep in-the-money European puts because of interest rates, and it is a reminder that this simple split is a teaching tool, not a pricing model. You will see what drives these numbers in Chapter 2.

body.title: Split the premium
body.prompt: The Nifty is at 25,300. The 25,000 call trades at ₹480. How much of that premium is time value, in rupees per unit?
body.explanation: Intrinsic value = max(25,300 − 25,000, 0) = ₹300. Time value = ₹480 − ₹300 = ₹180. If the Nifty is still at 25,300 on expiry day, this call will be worth ₹300 and the ₹180 will have vanished.

children.text: Expiry and Settlement: The Rules on NSE

markDefs.definition: An option that can only be exercised on its expiry date, not before. All NSE index and stock options are European style.

children.text: Every option has an expiry date, and after that it simply stops existing. All options on NSE are
European style
, so they settle on expiry day only. You can still sell your option in the market at any time before then, and most hedgers do exactly that rather than waiting for expiry.

stats.label: Nifty option expiry day
stats.context: Weekly every Tuesday. Monthly on the last Tuesday of the month

stats.label: Stock option expiries
stats.context: Last Tuesday of the month, no weekly contracts

stats.label: Index options settle in
stats.context: No shares change hands, only the profit or loss

stats.label: Stock options settle by
stats.context: In-the-money contracts at expiry mean real shares and real money

children.text: If expiry falls on a trading holiday, it moves to the previous trading day. Physical settlement of stock options matters a lot for hedgers. If Suresh's 1,450 Infosys put is in the money at expiry, he is treated as selling 400 shares at ₹1,450 and his broker will need those shares in his demat account. That can be fine, or it can be a surprise sale of a stock he wanted to keep. Chapter 5 covers how to handle this. For most hedgers, the simple rule is to close or roll a stock option before expiry week.

body.label: What an option buyer pays
body.context: Buying one lot of a Nifty put at ₹300 with a lot size of 65 costs ₹19,500, and that is the most the option itself can lose. Sellers instead block much larger margin, covered in Chapter 5.

body.title: Rights and obligations
body.textWithBlank: The buyer of an option has a right. The seller of that option has an ___.
body.explanation: The seller receives the premium in exchange for the obligation to buy (short put) or sell (short call) at the strike if the option ends in the money. That is why sellers must post margin and buyers do not.

children.text: The Wrong Button: What a Short Put Does to a Portfolio

body.caption: A short Nifty 25,000 put sold at ₹300. The most it can earn is the ₹300 premium. Below 24,700, it loses one rupee for every point the Nifty falls, exactly when a long-only portfolio is also losing.

body.title: The accidental seller
body.scenario: Lakshmi, 46, has ₹16 lakh in a Nifty 50 index fund. Before the Union Budget, with the Nifty at 25,000, she decides to hedge with one lot (65 units) of the monthly Nifty 25,000 put, trading at ₹300. In a hurry, she places a SELL order instead of a BUY. The order goes through and ₹19,500 is credited to her account. Two weeks later the Nifty is at 23,500.
body.prompt: What position does Lakshmi actually hold, and roughly what has happened to her combined portfolio? What should she learn from this?
body.modelAnswer:
1. She holds a short put: she has sold insurance, not bought it. She collected ₹19,500 in premium and took on the obligation to pay out if the Nifty falls below 25,000.
2. At 23,500, the put is ₹1,500 in the money, so its value is at least ₹1,500 × 65 = ₹97,500. It is probably a bit more with some time value left. Her short position has lost at least ₹97,500 − ₹19,500 = ₹78,000.
3. Her index fund, down about 6%, has lost roughly ₹96,000. Instead of a hedge reducing that loss, she is down about ₹1.74 lakh in total.
4. She would also have had a large amount of margin blocked from the moment the sell order went through, which is itself a warning sign she missed.
The lesson: a hedge always costs you money upfront. If you receive premium when you meant to protect yourself, stop and check the order immediately.

body.title: Why hedgers rarely sell uncovered options

children.text: Selling options feels attractive because the premium arrives immediately and most options do expire worthless. But the payoff is lopsided: small, frequent gains and occasional very large losses. That profile adds to the exact risk a long-only investor already carries. The two exceptions you will study in Chapter 4 both involve selling a call against something you already own:
Covered call: selling a call on shares you hold, so the obligation to sell is backed by the shares.
Collar: selling a call on shares you hold to help pay for a put that protects them.

body.title: Read a real option chain in ten minutes
steps: Open the NSE option chain or the option chain in your broker app, and select the Nifty and the nearest monthly expiry.
Find the strike closest to the current Nifty level and note the call and put premiums.
Pick one strike below the current level and work out the put's intrinsic value and time value.
Multiply that put premium by the current Nifty lot size to see what one lot of protection costs.
Switch to the next month's expiry and compare the premium for the same strike. Note how much more a longer expiry costs.

cards.definition: The right to buy the underlying at the strike price until expiry.
The right to sell the underlying at the strike price until expiry.
The seller of an option, who collects the premium and takes on the obligation.
What an option is worth if exercised now. Call: max(S − K, 0). Put: max(K − S, 0).
Premium minus intrinsic value. It decays to zero by expiry and is the real cost of a hedge.
Exercisable only on expiry day. All NSE options are European style.
Stock options that are in the money at expiry result in actual delivery of shares and money.

points: Calls are rights to buy and puts are rights to sell. Buyers pay premium for the right, sellers collect it and take on the obligation.
Of the four basic positions, the long put is the hedger's core tool. A short put adds crash risk and is not insurance.
A protective put caps the loss at the gap to the strike plus the premium, while keeping the upside.
Premium = intrinsic value + time value. Time value decays to zero by expiry, so it is the true cost of protection.
On NSE, Nifty options expire on Tuesdays and index options settle in cash. Stock options are monthly and physically settled.
If you receive premium when you meant to buy protection, you placed the wrong order.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Premiums, lot sizes and prices used here are illustrative, and exchange rules on expiry days and lot sizes change from time to time, so always check the latest NSE circulars. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before trading options.
